title: Interpret sampling distribution results in context
body: The mean, standard deviation, and probabilities for a sampling distribution of a sample proportion must be interpreted in the context of a specific population.
caution: Say clearly whether you mean the population, one sample of values, or the sample proportion across repeated samples. A vague "it" or "larger samples have less variability" can be read as the wrong one.
ced_evidence: 3.2.C.1 "should be interpreted in the context of a specific population"

title: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
caution: This formula uses the population proportion p. It applies when the sampled values are independent.

title: Mean of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
Identify the procedure and parameter for one proportion
body: The procedure for a confidence interval for one population proportion is a one-sample z-interval, and the parameter must name the proportion, the response variable, and the population in context.
caution: Define the parameter in words with the population from the problem. A bare symbol like p is not enough. For a hypothesis test the procedure is a one-sample z-test, and the parameter is described the same way.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.1 "one-sample z-interval for a population proportion"; 3.3.A.2 "reference the proportion, the response variable, and the population in context"

title: Interpreting the confidence level
body: A C% confidence level means that in repeated random sampling with the same sample size, approximately C% of the confidence intervals calculated will capture the population proportion.
caution: The confidence level describes the long-run capture rate of the method. It is not the probability that one computed interval contains the parameter. To interpret a specific interval, write "We are C% confident that the interval from a to b captures the [parameter in context]."
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.2 "approximately C% of confidence intervals calculated will capture the population proportion"; 3.4.A.3

title: Sample size and interval width
body: Increasing the sample size decreases the standard error, so with everything else unchanged the interval width tends to decrease, and it is approximately proportional to 1/\sqrt{n}.
ced_evidence: 3.4.C.2 "width of the interval is approximately proportional to 1/\sqrt{n}"

title: Justify a claim from a confidence interval
body: A confidence interval for a population proportion gives a range of plausible values, and it can serve as convincing evidence for a claim about the population proportion.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.1 "range of plausible values that may serve as convincing evidence"

title: Conclusion wording for a hypothesis test
body: State the conclusion in context, consistent with the alternative hypothesis, using non-definitive language, and refer to the parameter and population (or the populations).
caution: Never say "accept" or "prove" the null hypothesis. A large p-value means there is not convincing evidence for the alternative, which is different from evidence for the null. For chi-square tests, say the data do not provide convincing evidence of an association or a difference, rather than saying there is none.
ced_evidence: 3.7.B.6 "stated in context consistent with, and in terms of, the alternative hypothesis using non-definitive language"; 3.7.B.4; 3.13.C.3; 3.15.D.3

title: Mean of the sampling distribution of \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
caution: This applies to two independent populations when the sampled values are independent. Add the two variances under one radical. Do not subtract them or add the standard deviations.

title: Standard error of \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
ced_evidence: 3.10.D.1 "standard error (SE) for the difference between two population proportions"
